Good morning, and welcome to the seminar. Before we start, let me explain the question that will guide the whole semester. The use of algorithms by public agencies is not new. What is new is the scale. Today, a single system can make a million decisions in one day. If one of those decisions is wrong, the citizen has a right to a remedy. But if a million are wrong, we have a structural problem. So our question is not only who is responsible. It is how the law can guarantee accountability at that scale. Each week, two of you will present a paper, and I expect you to disagree with the authors at least once.

People think startups hate regulation. That is not true. What we hate is uncertainty. The lack of clear rules for high-risk systems is the biggest problem for companies like mine. Our system helps banks to make credit decisions. We test it for bias every month, and every decision has a human in the loop. But no regulator has told us exactly what level of explainability is enough. So our lawyers write long reports that nobody reads. My message to governments is simple: give us clear rules, give us one agency for oversight, and we will follow them.
